content.title: About
content.content: Beans (Phaseolus vulgaris) are edible seeds of the bean plant, cultivated worldwide. They have a mild, slightly nutty flavor and a firm, slightly creamy texture when cooked. Beans are eaten boiled, stewed, and used in salads, soups, and purees.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Beans belong to the legume family and are close relatives of peas, lentils, and soy.
There are more than 30 bean varieties differing in color, size, and taste.
Beans can fix nitrogen in the soil, improving its fertility.
In the 2020s beans became one of the fastest‑growing crops globally due to rising demand for plant protein.
Bean seeds are coated with a natural film containing phytic acid, which can reduce the absorption of some minerals.

items.title: Rich in plant protein
items.content: Beans contain about 20 % protein, making them a valuable protein source for vegetarians and vegans.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber in beans supports digestive health and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: Complex carbs provide steady energy and help regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Beans are a good source of folate, thiamine, and vitamin B6, important for metabolism.

items.title: Rich in minerals
items.content: Beans provide iron, magnesium, potassium, and zinc, essential for bodily functions.

items.title: Phytic acid content
items.content: Phytic acid can reduce iron and zinc absorption; soaking beans before cooking is recommended.

items.title: Toxic lectins
items.content: Raw beans contain lectins that can cause food poisoning; they must be cooked thoroughly.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to legumes.

items.title: Gas formation
items.content: Beans can cause increased gas in sensitive people.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Beans can be boiled, stewed, baked, or used as a puree (e.g., hummus). Add them to soups, salads, stews, and vegetarian patties. Soak beans for 8–12 hours, rinse, then cook until tender.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store dry beans in an airtight container in a cool, dry place; they keep well for up to a year. Cooked beans should be refrigerated and consumed within 4‑5 days.

chicken-drumstick-grilled-without-sauce-.title: Chicken drumstick, grilled without sauce, skin eaten

content.title: About
content.content: Chicken drumsticks are the lower part of the thigh, containing meat, skin and a small amount of bone. Grilled without sauce they retain the natural flavor of the meat, while the crisp skin adds aroma and texture.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chicken drumsticks are a staple in many world cuisines, from barbecue to Asian grill dishes.
Grilling without sauce makes the skin extra crunchy, enhancing the eating experience.
Chicken is one of the most affordable sources of high‑quality protein worldwide.
The iron content in chicken is higher than in beef of the same weight.
Drumsticks are often served “on the bone,” making them a convenient finger food.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Chicken drumsticks provide high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Source of vitamin B12
items.content: Vitamin B12 supports nervous system function and red blood cell formation.

items.title: Contains zinc
items.content: Zinc is important for immune health, wound healing, and DNA synthesis.

items.title: Low in carbohydrates
items.content: With virtually no carbs, drumsticks fit well into low‑carb and ketogenic diets.

items.title: Iron and selenium
items.content: These minerals provide antioxidant protection and support metabolism.

items.title: Risk of foodborne illness
items.content: Undercooked chicken may harbor Salmonella or Campylobacter; cook to an internal temperature of 75 °C.

items.title: High sodium in marinades
items.content: If the drumsticks were pre‑marinated, they can contain a lot of salt, which is a concern for hypertension.

items.title: Poultry allergy
items.content: A small number of people may have allergic reactions to chicken proteins.

items.title: Fat in the skin
items.content: Chicken skin is high in saturated fat; those monitoring cholesterol should consume it in moderation.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Eat the drumstick directly from the bone, pulling the meat away with your hands. The crisped skin adds flavor. Serve with vegetable sides, salads, or your favorite dipping sauces.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Fresh drumsticks keep in the refrigerator at 0–4 °C for up to 2 days. Frozen, they last up to 9 months. Thaw frozen pieces in the fridge before cooking, and store cooked leftovers in an airtight container for up to 3 days.

content.title: About
content.content: Hot chocolate made with low‑fat (1 %) or fat‑free (skim) milk is a beverage combining cocoa powder, sugar, and milk with very little fat. It retains a rich chocolate flavor while providing fewer calories and saturated fats than traditional hot chocolate made with whole milk.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Cocoa powder is rich in flavonoids, which have antioxidant properties.
Skim milk retains most of the protein and calcium but virtually no fat.
Hot chocolate originated in Mexico, where cacao was consumed by ancient civilizations.
In the United States hot chocolate is often topped with whipped cream, which is omitted in low‑fat versions.
Cocoa can be natural or Dutch‑processed, affecting color and acidity of the drink.

items.title: Rich in flavonoids
items.content: Flavonoids from cocoa support vascular function and reduce oxidative stress.

items.title: Source of calcium
items.content: Skim milk provides a high level of calcium essential for bone health.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: The drink typically contains less than 1 % fat, making it suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: Contains magnesium
items.content: Magnesium aids normal muscle and nerve function.

items.title: Mood‑enhancing
items.content: Cocoa stimulates serotonin and endorphin production, helping improve mood.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: People allergic to casein or lactose may react even to skim milk.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Hot chocolate often contains added sugar, which can raise the beverage’s glycemic index.

items.title: Caffeine and theobromine
items.content: Cocoa contains small amounts of caffeine and theobromine, which may affect sleep if consumed in large quantities.

items.title: Oxalates
items.content: Cocoa contains oxalates that, in excess, may contribute to kidney stone formation.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Heat the milk, add cocoa powder and sugar to taste, and whisk until smooth. Optional: stir in a pinch of vanilla or cinnamon for extra aroma. Serve hot, optionally topped with a dollop of whipped low‑fat cream.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cocoa powder in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. Keep skim milk refrigerated and use within 5–7 days after opening.

potato-salad-with-egg-made-with-light-ma.title: Potato Salad with Egg and Light Mayonnaise

content.title: About
content.content: Potato salad with egg and light mayonnaise is a classic dish popular in Russia and the CIS. It is made from boiled potatoes, hard‑boiled eggs, fresh vegetables (such as cucumbers and green onions) and a dressing based on light mayonnaise, which contains less fat than traditional mayonnaise.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The traditional recipe appeared in the early 20th century and quickly became a staple of festive tables.
Light mayonnaise usually contains 30‑40 % less fat, making the salad less caloric.
The salad is typically served cold, but it can be slightly warmed to enhance its aroma.
In some regions mustard or vinegar is added for a brighter flavor note.
Eggs add an extra source of protein, making the dish more filling.

items.title: Reduced fat content
items.content: Light mayonnaise lowers the overall fat and calorie count, which is beneficial for weight management.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Eggs and potatoes provide a complete set of amino acids, supporting muscle maintenance.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Eggs contain vitamin B12, while potatoes provide vitamin B6, both important for nervous system health.

items.title: Potassium and magnesium
items.content: Potatoes are a good source of potassium and magnesium, helping maintain normal blood pressure.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: Adding fresh vegetables increases fiber content, which aids digestion.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to eggs, ranging from skin rashes to anaphylaxis.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Light mayonnaise often contains added salt; people with hypertension should monitor intake.

items.title: Bacterial contamination
items.content: Salads containing boiled eggs should be refrigerated and consumed within 2‑3 days to prevent bacterial growth.

items.title: Potential calorie increase
items.content: Despite the light mayo, large portions can still add a significant amount of calories.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the salad chilled as an appetizer or side dish with meat. Garnish with fresh herbs, add mustard or lemon juice to taste. It pairs well with bread, fish, or a light soup.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the salad in an airtight container in the refrigerator at 0‑4 °C. Consume within 2‑3 days. Discard if it develops an off‑odor or discoloration.

content.title: About
content.content: Rice (Oryza sativa) is the edible grain of a cereal plant that was first domesticated in Asia thousands of years ago. It is a staple food for more than half of the world's population. Rice comes in many varieties, including white, brown, black, red, basmati, jasmine, and sticky rice, and it is eaten boiled, steamed, fried, or made into dishes such as pilaf, risotto, and congee.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Rice was domesticated in Asia, with evidence pointing to the Yangtze River region of China.
Brown rice is whole grain with its bran and germ; white rice has had them removed through milling.
Rice is grown in flooded fields called paddies in many regions.
Rice varieties are grouped by grain length: long, medium, and short.
Rice is naturally gluten-free.

items.title: Source of energy
items.content: Rice is rich in carbohydrates, which provide energy.

items.title: Brown rice provides fiber
items.content: Brown rice contains more fiber, magnesium, and manganese than white rice.

items.title: Often enriched
items.content: Enriched white rice may be fortified with B vitamins and iron.

items.title: Gluten-free
items.content: Rice is suitable for people who need to avoid gluten.

items.title: Easy to digest
items.content: White rice is mild and generally easy to digest.

items.title: Arsenic
items.content: Rice can absorb arsenic from soil and water. Eating a variety of grains and rinsing and cooking rice in plenty of water may reduce exposure.

items.title: Improperly stored cooked rice
items.content: Cooked rice left at room temperature can grow Bacillus cereus bacteria, which may cause food poisoning.

items.title: Glycemic effect
items.content: White rice can raise blood sugar quickly, so portions matter for people monitoring blood sugar.

items.title: Lower fiber in white rice
items.content: Refined white rice contains less fiber than whole grains.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Rice can be boiled or steamed and served as a side dish, in bowls, and in pilafs, risottos, sushi, stir-fries, and soups. Rinsing rice before cooking removes surface starch. Pairing rice with vegetables and protein makes a balanced meal.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store uncooked rice in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. White rice keeps for a long time, while brown rice, which contains oils, keeps for a shorter time. Cool cooked rice quickly, refrigerate it within about an hour, eat it within one to two days, and reheat it until it is steaming hot.

content.title: About
content.content: Dried seaweed (Seaweed, dried) is a dehydrated edible marine algae harvested from species such as nori, wakame, and kelp. It has a light oceanic aroma, a crisp texture, and a high nutritional density.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Seaweeds are among the oldest living organisms on Earth, existing for over 600 million years.
Dried seaweed is a staple in Asian cuisines: used in sushi, soups, salads, and as a seasoning.
Seaweeds accumulate iodine, making them one of the richest natural sources of this trace element.
In Japan, dried nori sheets are traditionally wrapped around rice for sushi rolls; in Korea, they are used in kimchi and soups.
When stored properly, dried seaweed can keep its nutrients for up to a year.

items.title: Rich in iodine
items.content: Iodine is essential for normal thyroid function and metabolic regulation.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Seaweed provides vitamin B12, rare in plant foods, as well as B6 and folate.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Carotenoids, vitamin C, and polyphenols help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports gut health
items.content: Dietary fibers such as pectin and alginate promote beneficial gut bacteria and aid digestion.

items.title: Low‑calorie snack
items.content: Dried seaweed is low in calories while delivering a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Excess iodine
items.content: Too much iodine can disrupt thyroid function, especially in individuals prone to hyperthyroidism.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Some dried seaweed products are salted; people with hypertension should choose unsalted versions.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: Rarely, some individuals may experience an allergy to marine algae.

items.title: Contaminants
items.content: Seaweed can accumulate heavy metals from the ocean; purchase from reputable sources.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Dried seaweed can be enjoyed as a snack, added to soups, salads, rice or noodle dishes, used as a seasoning powder (nori flakes), or rehydrated to make sushi rolls. A quick soak in warm water before use restores flexibility.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep dried seaweed in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. For extended storage, refrigerate to prevent moisture absorption and maintain crispness.
